title: Shimreishang Kala Maitonphi
title_translation: The Ballad of Shimreishang and Maitonphi
creator: Phungcham Oral Historians & Balladeers
author: Traditional
notes: Renowned 17th-century tragic romance ballad of Phungcham village. Preserves archaic dialect vocabulary, poetic meters, and bereavement mourning chants.
indigenous_tangkhul_text: Shimreishangna kaphung yarsho-li pamda, Maitonphi-wui samkapha leikashi ning-yanganung.
Luirim chonkashan shanaonao khamatha, Phungcham ramwui won thada ringkaphaphong.
Chitharan chikaning mava-likha, kharuikahao mayarnao kacham-kacham leikashi ngacheilaka.
I-leishatnao Maitonphi, nawui meikhangao thada iwui ningli ngasam-kahao mashunmana.
english_translation_text: Shimreishang sat gazing across the mountain slopes, yearning for the radiant beauty of Maitonphi.
Draped in the woven splendor of the Luirim shawl, she bloomed like the rarest wild flower of Phungcham.
Yet cruel fate and village clan divides intervened, testing the enduring devotion of the young lovers.
O my beloved Maitonphi, like the undying glow of embers, your memory finds no rest within my soul.
literary_themes: Tragic romance and star-crossed lovers (*Khararchan-Leikashi*)
Customary marriage negotiations and clan taboos
Poetic bereavement, mourning chants, and afterlife reunion in *Kazeiram*
Metaphorical imagery of mountain flora and traditional textiles
structure_and_meter: Epic ballad in traditional antiphonal meter with four-line stanzas and parallel rhythmic assonance.
critical_commentary: The quintessential national romantic epic of the Tangkhul people, composed in the 17th century in Phungcham village and transmitted through generations of oral balladeers.

poetic_vocabulary_terms.Luirim: Traditional prestigious red, white, and black striped woven shawl
poetic_vocabulary_terms.Kazeiram: The ancestral realm of the departed spirits
poetic_vocabulary_terms.Won: Blossom / flower / poetic metaphor for beauty and grace

title: Hao Khararchan: Tangkhul Folktales Collection
title_translation: Anthology of Tangkhul Ancestral Folktales
creator: Tangkhul Literature Society Editorial Board
author: Tangkhul Literature Society
notes: Comprehensive canonical anthology of ancestral Tangkhul folktales (Khararchan) compiled by native elders to preserve oral literature for school education.
indigenous_tangkhul_text: Hao khararchan-hi Tangkhul rali thot-kharewui khamashung tuingashit kashung akha.
Ava-apawui tharanli chithada shitsang-da, longshimli kakaso paonao-bingli pakhang shansangya.
Kaphung-kachon, ngatha-kazat, kala vare-khorumwui otshak kachiva hiyakha lairikli mathat-da lakahon.
english_translation_text: The ancestral folktales (*Hao Khararchan*) embody the wisdom and moral code of early Tangkhul generations.
Handed down by forefathers around the nocturnal hearth, these stories were taught to youth in village dormitories.
Mountain hunts, customary jurisprudence, and divine invocations are meticulously preserved within this collection.
literary_themes: Ancestral oral pedagogy and folklore transmission
Ethical justice, communal virtue, and retribution
Harmonious balance between humans, forest fauna, and nature spirits
Etiological myths explaining mountain landmarks and tribal origins
structure_and_meter: Prose folktale anthology with interspersed poetic chants (*Laa*) and ceremonial proverbs (*Paotam*).
critical_commentary: Compiled in 1981 by the Tangkhul Literature Society, this anthology codified centuries of unwritten oral lore into a canonical reader for community schools.

poetic_vocabulary_terms.Longshim: Traditional village youth dormitory and academy

title: Huikhayei Kala Sha
title_translation: The Story of the Dog and the Tiger
creator: Tangkhul Storytellers & S. Arokianathan
author: Traditional
publisher: Central Institute of Indian Languages, Mysore
notes: Classic animal fable explaining how the domestic dog became humanity's mountain hunting companion through cleverness and loyalty.
indigenous_tangkhul_text: Thot-khareli Huikhayei kala Sha maranao thada kaphungli ngaso-kacham pama.
Huina Shali matuida khangayei ning-kakhon matuida mayar-pamli chotchan-da miwui shimlut sanga.
Hithada Huikhayei mishi kaphara-eili mi-wui ngachee kaphaning kala kashap pan-kaso shansangya.
english_translation_text: In ancient times, the Dog (*Huikhayei*) and the Tiger (*Sha*) lived together as brothers roaming the high mountain ridges.
Recognizing the superior intellect and mastery of humankind, the clever dog chose to seek domestic fellowship with man.
Thus the dog became humanity's loyal companion, guarding the household and guiding the village hunter through the wild.
literary_themes: Animal fable and etiology of animal domestication
Foresight, clever adaptability, and pragmatic loyalty
The contrast between untamed wilderness (*Ngashim*) and village civilization (*Ram*)
structure_and_meter: Allegorical prose narrative featuring dialogue and trickster motifs with an epigrammatic moral conclusion.
critical_commentary: A classic Tibeto-Burman animal fable documented by S. Arokianathan in 1982, illustrating how indigenous oral literature explains ecological relationships.

poetic_vocabulary_terms.Sha: Tiger / wild predator of the forest

title: Kashunao wui Khararchan
title_translation: The Tale of the Orphan Boy
creator: Tangkhul Oral Tradition Custodians
author: Traditional
notes: Widespread traditional moral tale of an impoverished orphan boy who triumphs over adversity through customary virtue, patience, and ancestral blessings.
indigenous_tangkhul_text: Kashunao akhana shim-khamachamli pamda ava-apa makhavai kacham-kacham pharora.
Kachang-khalia mibingna athishangli mashak kachi-eili, ningteotet-da Vare-li khorum-kachang makhayipmana.
Kashukwui tharanli awungana athishangli khamatha shanao mi-da wungnao shansangya.
english_translation_text: A poor orphan boy lived in quiet solitude, bereft of parents and enduring severe mountain hardships.
Though the proud and wealthy mocked his threadbare clothes, his spirit remained humble and steadfast in prayer.
In the fullness of time, the village chief rewarded his upright virtue by giving him his daughter's hand and noble rank.
literary_themes: The orphan archetype (*Kashunao*) as a moral exemplar in indigenous folklore
Triumph of virtue, diligence, and humility over arrogance
Divine intervention and customary social mobility through marriage
structure_and_meter: Tripartite folktale structure: trial and deprivation, magical/moral test, and social elevation.
critical_commentary: The orphan motif is universally cherished across Naga cultures as a reflection on social justice, community empathy, and spiritual reward for moral perseverance.

poetic_vocabulary_terms.Vare-Khorum: Reverent prayer and trust in the Supreme Creator
poetic_vocabulary_terms.Wungnao: Nobility / honored status in the village council

title: The Legend of Mount Shirui and Kashongwui Won
title_translation: The Origin Legend of the Sentinel Peak and its Blossom
creator: Shirui Community Custodians & M. Horam
author: Traditional
notes: Ancestral cosmological legend narrating the spiritual union between the guardian spirit of Shirui mountain and the rare mountain lily (Lilium mackliniae).
indigenous_tangkhul_text: Shirui Kashong kaphungli Princess Philavana cloud-dwelling spirits-wui ngachonli pamya.
Kashongwui Won (Shirui Lily) Philavawui kaphara leishat kala modesty-wui kashik thada bloom sakya.
Kaphung crest-li windswept mist-li pharak-da kaza-khangao leikashi ancestral folklore-li ngari-shitsangya.
english_translation_text: Atop the windswept crags of Mount Shirui, the spirit princess Philava dwelt amidst swirling cloud guardians.
The sacred flower of the peak (*Kashongwui Won*) bloomed as an eternal witness to her unblemished beauty and modesty.
Encased in alpine mist, this ecological wonder has inspired centuries of poetic reverence and mythological devotion.
literary_themes: Cosmological animism and nature spirit guardians (*Philava*)
Sacred landscape personification and alpine ecology
The flower as a symbol of feminine purity, regional pride, and mystery
structure_and_meter: Mythological narrative incorporating nature hymnody, descriptive topographic verse, and ritual invocations.
critical_commentary: Recorded by anthropologist M. Horam in 1977, this legend bridges Tangkhul cosmology with the unique ecological marvel of the endemic Shirui Lily.

poetic_vocabulary_terms.Kashongwui Won: The flower of the peak (Shirui Lily / Lilium mackliniae)
poetic_vocabulary_terms.Philava: Mythical guardian princess and spirit protector of Mount Shirui

title: Kachakui Kala Shanao
title_translation: The Crow and the Pheasant
creator: TLS Primary Curriculum Committee
author: Traditional
notes: Moral fable for children explaining the plumages of birds and warning against jealousy, pride, and greed. Published in Class IV textbook Zingyar Tangkhul.
indigenous_tangkhul_text: Thotli Kachakui (Crow) kala Shanao (Pheasant) khani akha-akha-li paint sak-kacham tuingashitya.
Shanaona Kachakuili black soot-li marikta chapa-khavai kachon mathat-da shapkasa sakya.
Kachakuina ningkhamachap-da Shanaowui plumages-li colorful spots mathat-da lakahon, ngashan hithada pharora.
english_translation_text: Once, the Crow (*Kachakui*) and the Pheasant (*Shanao*) made a covenant to paint each other's feathers with splendor.
The pheasant patiently decorated the crow with deep glossy soot, taking great care to craft an elegant garment.
Yet the impatient crow splashed colors hastily, giving the pheasant its spotted plumage and ending their brotherhood.
literary_themes: Children's moral fable on patience versus impetuous greed
Etiological explanation of bird plumage and animal characteristics
The sacredness of keeping promises and fulfilling reciprocal duties
structure_and_meter: Playful educational prose with simple sentence syntax and repetitive dialogue designed for elementary readers.
critical_commentary: Published in the official Class IV Tangkhul textbook Zingyar Tangkhul (2022) to teach foundational moral principles through ancestral avian stories.

title: Sikui Kala Machun
title_translation: The Deer and the Crab
creator: TLS Primary Curriculum Committee
author: Traditional
notes: Classic humorous trickster story contrasting the swift deer with the patient, resourceful crab. Published in Class II textbook Wontui Tangkhul.
indigenous_tangkhul_text: Sikui (Deer) na Machun (Crab)-li racing-li challenge sakda, 'Nakhurli pamkaza, iwui speed mashapmana!' hithada tuitsang.
Machunna clever-laka da Sikuiwui kachei-li khangarom-da finish line-li advance-da phungchan.
Kacham-kacham mibingna speed-wui matuida clever strategy kala patience-na victory shansangya.
english_translation_text: The swift Deer (*Sikui*) challenged the slow Crab (*Machun*) to a race, mocking: 'Creeping in the mud, you can never match my stride!'
Yet the astute crab clung discreetly to the deer's tail, tumbling forward across the finish line first with quiet composure.
Thus children learn that unbridled pride is outmatched by clever foresight, resourcefulness, and calm patience.
literary_themes: The classic trickster fable: slow wits versus rapid agility
Humility and the folly of boastful overconfidence
Resourceful problem-solving in challenging situations
structure_and_meter: Short humorous fable with dynamic narrative pacing and dialogue, followed by a pedagogic summary.
critical_commentary: Curated in the Class II primary reader Wontui Tangkhul (2022), this story teaches young children that wit and steadiness overcome sheer physical strength.

poetic_vocabulary_terms.Sikui: The wild barking deer of the mountain forests
poetic_vocabulary_terms.Machun: The river crab dwelling in rocky mountain streams

title: Ava Ram Leishat
title_translation: Love of the Motherland
creator: Luingam A. Shimray
author: Luingam A. Shimray
notes: Celebrated modern Tangkhul lyric poem praising the beauty, verdant ridges, and cultural spirit of the ancestral hills. Included in Class IX textbook Tangkhul Tuitam Kachiko.
indigenous_tangkhul_text: I-ram Hunphun, I-ram Ukhrul, kaphung yarsho-wui shimlut kashak,
Varenana kapha rali ringsang-da, ngasot-mayarnao makhayipmana.
Ava Ram leishatna iwui ngalungli meikha thada meikhangao,
Thot kachivali nawui ming-kachon kaphung kachivali pakhang shitsangya.
english_translation_text: My homeland Hunphun, my beloved Ukhrul, majestic citadel along the mountain crest,
Where the Creator poured forth bounties, and comrades dwell in unbroken fellowship.
Love of the Motherland burns like living fire within the deepest chambers of my soul,
Through all the ages, your honored name shall echo across every ancestral ridge.
literary_themes: Patriotic devotion to the ancestral mountain homeland (*Ava Ram*)
Celebration of high altitude topography, verdant ridges, and pristine springs
Cultural continuity and inter-generational solidarity
structure_and_meter: Modern lyrical verse composed in regular four-line stanzas with heroic cadence and end-rhymes.
critical_commentary: Authored by Luingam A. Shimray and anthologized in Class IX textbook Tangkhul Tuitam Kachiko (2000), this poem is one of the most widely recited anthems of Tangkhul identity.

poetic_vocabulary_terms.Ngasot: Camaraderie and lifelong fellowship among clan youth

title: Kachamwui Meikha
title_translation: Embers of Poverty
creator: Y.K. Shimray
author: Y.K. Shimray
notes: Reflective modern lyric poem exploring mountain social hardship, moral perseverance, and the dignity of rural farm laborers. Published in Class XI textbook Wordham Tuitam Khare.
indigenous_tangkhul_text: Kachamwui meikhana kaphung chimli lumkaza makhaleiya tharan,
Mayarnao kharashotna terrace luili kashak ot-phun shitsangya.
Tara kashung-eili ning-khikhara, Varewui blessing kachivali ringpha kashung,
Hina Tangkhul mibingwui resilience kala dignified survival-wui kashik.
english_translation_text: When the embers of poverty provide meager warmth in the chilly mountain winter,
The resilient laborer climbs to the terraced fields, bearing the heavy yoke of toil.
Though tears may mingle with sweat, trusting gratitude to the Almighty brings quiet joy,
For this is the enduring testament of Tangkhul fortitude and dignified survival.
literary_themes: Social realism and empathetic depiction of rural poverty
The dignity of agrarian labor and terraced cultivation
Resilience, spiritual fortitude, and enduring hope amidst hardship
structure_and_meter: Reflective elegiac poetry in free-flowing stanzas utilizing tactile thermal imagery (cold mist, glowing embers).
critical_commentary: Composed by Y.K. Shimray for Class XI Wordham Tuitam Khare (2021), this piece represents modern Tangkhul literary realism addressing contemporary mountain socio-economic realities.

poetic_vocabulary_terms.Meikha: Glowing embers of the hearth / inner spark of survival
poetic_vocabulary_terms.Kharashot: Enduring grueling labor with quiet dignity
poetic_vocabulary_terms.Lui-Ot: The sacred labor of paddy terrace cultivation

title: Shirui Kashongwui Won
title_translation: Flower of Mount Shirui
creator: T. Luikham
author: T. Luikham
notes: Evocative ode celebrating the delicate bloom of the Shirui Lily, using ecological imagery as a metaphor for modesty, beauty, and endurance. Published in Class X Tuitam Kathara.
indigenous_tangkhul_text: Kashong yarsho-li Philavawui won, delicate pink-white bloom kachara,
Windswept crest-li proud thada shoka, nature-wui rarest jewel lakahon.
Nawui modesti kala quiet majesty, Tangkhul shanao-wui virtue thada pama,
Thot kachivali Shirui kaphungna nawui purity protect sakya.
english_translation_text: Upon the jagged ridge of the peak blooms the lily of Princess Philava, tender in pink and white hues,
Standing proud against alpine winds, celebrated as nature's most precious jewel.
Your modesty and quiet majesty reflect the graceful virtue of Tangkhul maidenhood,
Through all the changing seasons, Mount Shirui cradles and protects your sacred purity.
literary_themes: Ecological ode and celebration of the endemic flora
Metaphorical pairing of the lily with indigenous feminine modesty and virtue
The mountain summit as a fortress of natural and spiritual sanctity
structure_and_meter: Lyrical ode in rhymed quatrains with rich sensory imagery evoking alpine breezes, dew, and granite crags.
critical_commentary: Written by pioneer educationist and lexicographer T. Luikham and anthologized in Class X Tuitam Kathara (2021), this ode is celebrated for its musicality and ecological symbolism.

title: Ngashan Kathara
title_translation: The New Dawn
creator: S. Kanrei
author: S. Kanrei
notes: Visionary modernist poem exploring community renaissance, literacy advancement, and cultural self-determination in the post-independence era. Published in Class XII Wordham Tuitam Kakhane.
indigenous_tangkhul_text: Ngashan Katharana kaphung kachivali ngakhayei zingsho kakhon,
Lairik pakhang, tuitam khamathan, kala community solidarity ngathur-shitsangya.
Ancient values kala modern education ngarum-da future-wui path shurda,
Iram Tangkhul progressive nationhood-wui horizon-li phungchan.
english_translation_text: The New Dawn (*Ngashan Kathara*) breaks across every mountain crest, banishing the shadows of old,
Universal literacy, grammatical refinement, and community solidarity march hand in hand.
Uniting ancestral virtues with modern enlightenment, our youth tread the path of wisdom,
Guiding the Tangkhul nation toward a prosperous and unified horizon.
literary_themes: Cultural renaissance, literacy enlightenment, and social renewal
Synthesizing ancestral customs (*Ngashan*) with modern education
Visionary hope for youth leadership, tribal self-determination, and unity
structure_and_meter: Modernist blank verse with elevated rhetorical diction, energetic pacing, and prophetic rhythm.
critical_commentary: Composed by S. Kanrei for Class XII Wordham Tuitam Kakhane (2021), this poem encapsulates the intellectual optimism of modern Tangkhul literature.

poetic_vocabulary_terms.Ngashan Kathara: The new dawn / modern cultural renaissance
poetic_vocabulary_terms.Zingsho: The rising dawn light / radiant sunrise
poetic_vocabulary_terms.Ngarum-Kashung: Collective unity in achieving communal goals

title: Shongza
title_translation: Shongza: A Tangkhul Drama
creator: Tangkhul Literature Society Dramatic Board
author: Tangkhul Literature Society
notes: Major full-length theatrical drama written for undergraduate literature studies, addressing customary clan dispute arbitration, youth romance, and modern social reconciliation.
indigenous_tangkhul_text: Scene 1: Hangva elders council meets at the village sanctuary to arbitrate a disputed terraced border.
Shongzana mayarnao-bingli customary law (Ngashan) kala peaceful mediation-wui virtue interpret sakya.
Customary oaths (Lung-Kashun) kala ancestral covenants-na village warfare-wui tragedy avert sakya.
Dialogue balances classical oratorical Tangkhul with realistic village colloquial idiom.
english_translation_text: Act I: The council of elders (*Hangva*) convenes at the village assembly ground to arbitrate a boundary conflict.
Shongza, the noble mediator, passionately articulates the sanctity of customary jurisprudence and peace.
Through sacred stone covenants (*Lung-Kashun*), clan vengeance is averted and harmony restored.
The dramatic dialogue balances dignified classical rhetoric with lively, authentic village speech.
literary_themes: Traditional customary jurisprudence (*Ngashan*) and peaceful conflict resolution
The role of the orator-mediator (*Shongza*) in community welfare
The sacredness of land boundaries and ancestral oaths
structure_and_meter: Three-act theatrical stage play featuring structured dramatic conflict, choral interludes, and oratorical monologues.
critical_commentary: Commissioned by the Tangkhul Literature Society Dramatic Board in 2007 for collegiate study, Shongza is widely recognized as a masterwork of modern indigenous drama.

poetic_vocabulary_terms.Shongza: The noble orator, peacemaker, and customary judicial advocate
poetic_vocabulary_terms.Hangva: Village elder council and judicial tribunal
poetic_vocabulary_terms.Lung-Kashun: Sacred stone covenant marking inviolable boundaries

title: Maitonphi: A Dramatic Adaptation
title_translation: Verse-Drama of Maitonphi and Shimreishang
creator: Tangkhul Dramatic Troupe & TLS
author: Tangkhul Literature Society
notes: Stage play adaptation of the northern Tangkhul tragic love narrative, structured in five acts preserving traditional dialogue and song interludes.
indigenous_tangkhul_text: Act III: Maitonphi weaves the ceremonial Luirim cloth at her backstrap loom while singing an elegiac lament.
Shimreishang arrives at dusk, pledging undying devotion before departing on a perilous distant expedition.
The dramatic chorus echoes traditional folk song melodies (Pheichak Laa) commenting on fate's unyielding decree.
english_translation_text: Act III: Maitonphi weaves the ceremonial Luirim shawl at her backstrap loom, singing a haunting song of longing.
Shimreishang arrives at dusk, declaring his eternal devotion before departing on a perilous frontier journey.
The chorus chants antiphonal folk refrains, reflecting on the inexorable tragedy of human destiny.
literary_themes: Theatrical dramatization of the 17th-century Phungcham tragic romance
Integration of folk songs, weaving chants, and backstrap loom rhythms into stage performance
Tension between clan duties and individual emotional devotion
structure_and_meter: Five-act verse drama with alternating spoken dialogue, choral antiphony, and lyrical monologues.
critical_commentary: Adapted by the Tangkhul Dramatic Troupe and published by TLS in 1995, this play has been staged in community auditoriums across Ukhrul and Imphal to acclaim.

poetic_vocabulary_terms.Luirim-Tak: The rhythmic art of weaving the ceremonial shawl
poetic_vocabulary_terms.Kharashot-Laa: Elegiac song of enduring longing and sorrow
poetic_vocabulary_terms.Yarsho: Mountain path taken by travelers and warriors
poetic_vocabulary_terms.Ning-Khamathan: Pure and faithful devotion of the heart

title: Maranwon
title_translation: The Blossom of Fate
creator: R. Shaiza
author: R. Shaiza
notes: Influential modern realistic short story depicting village familial bonds, migration choices, and traditional mountain ethical resilience. Anthologized in Class IX Tangkhul Tuitam Kachiko.
indigenous_tangkhul_text: Maranwonna village school-li teaching sakda rural education-wui vang dedicated service shitsangya.
Town-li migration opportunity khalei-eili, ancestral village-li youth training-wui duty choose sakya.
Story-na traditional communal values kala modern urban aspirations-wui conflict realistically depict sakya.
english_translation_text: Maranwon dedicated her life to teaching in her native village school, guiding children toward enlightenment.
Though alluring opportunities urged her to migrate to the distant city, she chose to remain anchored to her ancestral soil.
The narrative realistically portrays the poignant choice between modern individual careerism and indigenous community duty.
literary_themes: Mountain education and rural community service as ethical callings
Tension between rural homeland roots and urban outward migration
Female agency, dedication, and moral leadership in modern hill society
structure_and_meter: Realistic short story with chronological narrative arc, psychological character depth, and evocative setting details.
critical_commentary: Authored by R. Shaiza and anthologized in Class IX Tangkhul Tuitam Kachiko (2000), this story has sparked decades of classroom discussions on rural development.

poetic_vocabulary_terms.Maranwon: Literary name signifying 'the blossom of destiny'
poetic_vocabulary_terms.Lairik-Kakaso: The sacred calling of educational instruction

poetic_vocabulary_terms.Otkhare: Selfless service and noble civic action

title: Kasomwoshi wui Shim
title_translation: Kasomwoshi's Homestead
creator: K.S. Kasomwoshi
author: K.S. Kasomwoshi
notes: Social realism short story portraying the transition of traditional village agriculture and household economy in the late 20th century.
indigenous_tangkhul_text: Kasomwoshina ancestral homestead-li pamda terraced farming, cattle rearing, kala traditional crafts protect sakya.
Modern cash economy advance-eili, traditional barter (khamasit) kala barter-market customs transition depict sakya.
Shim-wui sanctity, elders-wui wisdom, kala sustainable ecological living-wui philosophy shitsangya.
english_translation_text: Kasomwoshi tended his ancestral homestead with steadfast care, maintaining terraced fields, cattle, and woodcrafts.
As the modern cash economy penetrated the hills, he witnessed the gradual transformation of traditional mutual aid.
The story honors the sanctity of the family hearth, the wisdom of village elders, and sustainable ecological living.
literary_themes: Socio-economic transformation of mountain agrarian livelihoods
The homestead (*Shim*) as the physical and spiritual anchor of kinship
Preserving traditional ecological wisdom amidst rapid modernization
structure_and_meter: Gentle realistic prose characterized by ethnographic authenticity, detailed domestic description, and quiet philosophical humor.
critical_commentary: Published by K.S. Kasomwoshi in 1991, this work stands as a poignant documentation of Tangkhul village domestic life during the late 20th-century transition.

poetic_vocabulary_terms.Shim: Ancestral household, dwelling place, and lineage sanctuary
poetic_vocabulary_terms.Khamasit: Mutual cooperative labor sharing across village households
poetic_vocabulary_terms.Ringkaphaphong: Sustained peace, health, and holistic flourishing

title: Yarnao wui Akhama
title_translation: The Morning of the Labor Exchange
creator: V. Ruivah
author: V. Ruivah
notes: Short story depicting communal terrace paddy cultivation, youth camaraderie in the Yarnao labor group, and the rhythm of mountain village life.
indigenous_tangkhul_text: Akhama dawn mist-li Yarnao youth labor group-na drum and song-li terraced fields-li march sakya.
Mayarnao kala shanaonao communal paddy transplantation (Luisak)-li rhythmically toil sakda fellowship foster sakya.
Mutual aid, youth humor, folk singing, kala agricultural festivity vibrant thada narrative-li captured.
english_translation_text: In the cool morning mist, the youth cooperative labor band (*Yarnao*) marched toward the terraced fields singing in unison.
Young men and maidens transplanted green seedlings (*Luisak*) in rhythmic coordination, sharing laughter and songs.
The narrative captures the vibrant camaraderie, witty banter, and communal harmony of traditional mountain agriculture.
literary_themes: Communal agricultural labor groups (*Yarnao*) as the heartbeat of village society
Antiphonal singing and rhythmic synchronization in manual farm work
Romantic courting and youthful wit amidst communal toil
structure_and_meter: Vivid atmospheric short story capturing the sounds, sensory smells, and energetic rhythm of a single agricultural workday.
critical_commentary: Authored by anthropologist and literary writer V. Ruivah in 1993, this story provides an invaluable literary depiction of traditional cooperative labor institutions.

poetic_vocabulary_terms.Yarnao: Youth peer labor collective for mutual farm work
poetic_vocabulary_terms.Akhama: Dawn twilight / the fresh morning hour
poetic_vocabulary_terms.Luisak: Ceremonial transplanting of green paddy seedlings

title: Tangkhul Folk Literature Anthology
title_translation: Anthology of Tangkhul Folklore, Ballads, and Proverbs
creator: S. Arokianathan
author: S. Arokianathan
publisher: Central Institute of Indian Languages, Mysore
notes: Seminal scholarly anthology published under CIIL Folklore Series documenting Tangkhul oral narratives, courting songs, funeral dirges, proverbs, and riddles with linguistic commentary.
indigenous_tangkhul_text: Central Institute of Indian Languages (CIIL) Mysore-na 1982-li Tangkhul Folk Literature monograph publish sakya.
Dr. S. Arokianathan-na oral narratives, folk ballads (Maitonphi), dirges, riddles, kala proverbs document sakya.
Phonetic transcription, English translations, kala structural linguistic analysis comprehensive-laka sanga.
english_translation_text: In 1982, the Central Institute of Indian Languages (CIIL) in Mysore published this definitive Tangkhul Folk Literature monograph.
Compiled by Dr. S. Arokianathan, it systematically documented oral tales, the ballad of Maitonphi, proverbs, and riddles.
Featuring IPA phonetic transcriptions and interlinear English translations, it remains a landmark of academic linguistic folklore.
literary_themes: Comprehensive scientific documentation of oral literature genres
Preservation of archaic dialects (Phungcham, Ukhrul, Champhung)
Linguistic, metric, and syntactic analysis of traditional verbal art
structure_and_meter: Multilingual scholarly monograph containing bilingual texts, phonetic notations, structural tables, and glossaries.
critical_commentary: The premier academic anthology of Tangkhul oral verbal art, establishing standard methodology for Tibeto-Burman folklore documentation.

poetic_vocabulary_terms.Folk-Literature: Indigenous oral lore, verbal art, and narrative tradition
poetic_vocabulary_terms.Paochirun: Traditional poetic riddles and witty word-games
poetic_vocabulary_terms.Khararchan-Laa: Ballad poetry set to traditional melodies

title: Tangkhul Tuitam Kachiko
title_translation: Tangkhul Literature Reader for Class IX
creator: Tangkhul Literature Society Editorial Board

title: Hangkho Khalángwui Khararchan
title_translation: The Tale of the Boy Who Became a Hornbill
creator: Tangkhul Oral Tradition Custodians & Storytellers
author: Traditional
publisher: Tangkhul Literature Society / Documented in Arokianathan 1982
notes: Poignant ancestral folktale of the mistreated orphan boy Hangkho who crafted wings of hornbill feathers and transformed into the great hornbill.
indigenous_tangkhul_text:
Kashunao mayarnao Hangkho akha pamlaga, akhava eina ava kathinao-wui vangli kacham-kacham khangaran shurui.
Chitharan ava-nganungna khamakhei shimchin pida, sangkhor-li pamkakhung eina khararchan ning-ngachailaka.

Iramwui vanao kachiphun thada iwui khamahon horkhava ningungda, akhan akhang eina vanao wui mashon phapha-khavai.
Phungcham ramwui khararchar-li vanao-wui khon sakakhung eina, 'Hangkho-nao vanao khangaran!' da makhawor-lakmana.

Mei-ngaleili kapam mayarnao Hangkho, kazingramwui mashon phaphakhavai khurkhava-li kakhayei vanao wui mashan zatta.
Chiwui thada kachamnao mayarnao Hangkho khalángwui khon horkashung eina phung-ngathang kazingli khaláng-haowa.
english_translation_text:
In an ancient village lived the orphan boy Hangkho, who suffered endless cruelty and neglect after the passing of his parents.
Treated harshly by his stepmother and relegated to the cold hearth, he wept silently beneath the shadow of the mountain ridge.

Yearning to escape human torment like the free-flying birds of the alpine forest, he gathered fallen feathers day by day.
Weaving wings of hornbill plumage, he climbed to the highest ridge of Phungcham and cried aloud: 'Hangkho has taken flight!'

Leaving behind the earthly hearth and village sorrows, he spread his great feathers toward the boundless azure sky.
Thus the orphan boy transformed into the majestic great hornbill, soaring forever across the sacred mountain peaks.
literary_themes: Orphan adversity and cruelty of uncustomary stepmother (*Kashunao wui Khangaran*)
Avian metamorphism and transformation into the Great Hornbill (*Vanao Khaláng*)
Yearning for celestial freedom and spiritual liberation from village bondage
The moral obligation of community solidarity and defense of vulnerable youth
structure_and_meter: Ancestral mythological narrative in tri-partite tragic meter with rhythmic refrain and sorrow chants.
critical_commentary: One of the most famous and deeply poignant folktales in the Tangkhul canon. It warns community members against the mistreatment of orphans and poetically portrays the hornbill as a symbol of transcendent ancestral spirits.

title: Thānglongphi wui Khararchan
title_translation: The Legend and Ballad of Lady Thānglongphi
creator: Hungpung & Phungcham Oral Balladeers
author: Traditional
publisher: Documented in Horam 1977, Tangkhul Literature Society
notes: Celebrated epic romance ballad of Lady Thānglongphi of Hungpung, exemplifying feminine grace, aristocratic nobility, and tragic fidelity.
indigenous_tangkhul_text:
Hungpung ramwui shanaonao khamatha Thānglongphi, luirim kachon shanchingda ngashan mirin kazatta.
Phungcham, Hunphun, kala Shirui mayarnaona thāda iwui ning-leishat kapha samphangkhavai kharui-kacham sakashung.

Amei-ngalāwui khamathei thada mayon-kazat Thānglongphi, kacham-kacham leishat-wui mangli kashak-kakhayei leilaka.
Khamashung leishat eina ramwui ngashan kakharak eili, chitheikhamei ning-khangao ningchot-chot sakahaowa.

Thānglongphiwui khararchan hi Tangkhul shanao-wui khamatha kala ning-kachamwui kachungkha kapikathat phaphong.
Kazeiram vana kaphunga ramli thāda iwui leikashi makhangashit thada meikha shurda kapamhaowa.
english_translation_text:
In the ancestral village of Hungpung lived Lady Thānglongphi, celebrated across all northern valleys for her incomparable grace.
Draped in the crimson and black stripes of the sacred Luirim shawl, young suitors from Phungcham and Shirui vied for her heart.

Yet like the rarest mountain blossom that flourishes beside the cliff, her radiant beauty brought both admiration and tragic rivalries.
Bound by customary inter-village alliances and clan pledges, she was caught between true romantic devotion and clan duties.

The epic legend of Thānglongphi endures as a celebrated testimony to womanly virtue, steadfast courage, and tragic fate.
Her memory remains etched in Tangkhul oral memory, sung around hearthsides when winter mists blanket the mountain terraces.
literary_themes: Legendary romance and female nobility (*Shanao Khamatha*)
Inter-village marital pacts and customary clan negotiations
Tragic romantic destiny and steadfast fidelity
Traditional Tangkhul textiles (Luirim) as motifs of status and moral beauty
structure_and_meter: Elegiac oral ballad in rhythmic couplets with alternating choral responses and village praise tags.
critical_commentary: Complementing the ballad of Maitonphi, the story of Thānglongphi is a classic chronicle of feminine poise and aristocratic virtue in feudal Tangkhul society, highlighting the profound emotional weight of customary kinship bonds.

title: Marānao eina Kazing Philava wui Khararchan
title_translation: The Orphan Cowherd and the Queen of the Sky
creator: Tangkhul Oral Tradition Custodians
author: Traditional
publisher: Central Institute of Indian Languages, Mysore
notes: Mythological oral romance narrating the union and tragic parting between a humble cowherd boy and a celestial princess.
indigenous_tangkhul_text:
Marānao mayarnao seishatpamli seikhur kachikhangai, kazing kaphunga eili phaphung-won khamatha mayonzatta.
Chitharan kazing-chiko kashungli Kazing Philavana meikaphara mashon eina seipam-li ngur-ngur tonda kashun.

Marānaona kayei-kaphung ngareili Philavawui kachon shimkhuilaga, 'Inangli ngakhunmila, iwui ramli ngasamphang-lu!' da marui.
Kazing Philavana marānao kachamnaowui ning-leishat theida, ngaleili pamlaga thithang shimwui kapha kaphara ser-manda.

Kha kachung-chihui ngacheilaga kazing mashon kachon samphanglaga, Philavana kaphung-kazing ramli ngaláng-haowa.
Marānaona kazeiram kala kazing ngalei mangayapda, ngasam-kakha mangli leishat khon horda meingap-pamhaowa.
english_translation_text:
An impoverished cowherd boy watched his cattle upon the mountain grasslands where wild lilies bloomed beneath the clouds.
At the mystical hour of dusk, the Celestial Maiden (Queen of the Heavens) descended in a cloak of starlight to bathe in the spring.

The cowherd hid her celestial feathered robe and whispered: 'Abide with me in this earthly home, and be my beloved companion.'
Moved by his humble gentleness and genuine devotion, she dwelt with him upon the earth, blessing his homestead with abundance.

Yet after many moons, finding her concealed celestial robe beneath the granary, she was summoned back to the starry heavens.
The cowherd looked up into the twilight sky with unending longing, his hearth-song forever carrying the melody of celestial love.
literary_themes: Celestial-terrestrial romantic union (*Kazing eina Ngalei Leikashi*)
The magic feather robe motif (*Mashon Kachon*) common to world folklore
Humble virtue rewarded by divine favor and agricultural prosperity
Inevitable separation between mortal earth and the eternal sky realm
structure_and_meter: Mythological oral romance in episodic narrative stanzas with lyrical pastoral interludes.
critical_commentary: A canonical Tangkhul iteration of the celestial maiden folktale. It explores the tension between earthly mortal existence and transcendent divine beauty, celebrating the purity of the impoverished cowherd's spirit.

title: Kongyang wui Khararchan
title_translation: The Story of the Cicada and the Lean Season
creator: Tangkhul Storytellers & TLS Elementary Board
author: Traditional
notes: Classic didactic animal fable illustrating the virtues of foresight, agricultural diligence, and seasonal preparation in mountain villages.
indigenous_tangkhul_text:
Chikaning akhali ramli chiyan-ngachon kashung eina, kongyangna thing-phangli pamda laa khamatha seiser-kazatta.
Chitharan yarwui mayarnaona phangyāngli luikakhui eili mashun-mashun khangaran sakashung.

Kongyangna ning-ngalungli 'Yarsho kachikha thithang meingaláng, khipana maringphang kaji maleimana' da phanit-kazatta.
Kha kachikhangai yarthang vashungli mei-kacham eina kazing kaho rorkhavai, kongyangli kachama kashang maleikahaowa.

Luilap kashung eili kongyangna yarwui mayarnaoli 'Ili kachama mikhuilu!' da marui kha mayarnaona makhaning.
Kongyangwui khararchan hi kakhayak khangarang kala luingao khangashan-wui pangkakha thada Tangkhul ramli karamtatta.
english_translation_text:
During the radiant season of spring, the cicada sat upon the oak branches, singing sweet melodies throughout the sunny days.
Meanwhile, the diligent youth of the village laboured under the scorching sun, clearing hillside terraces and planting paddy.

The cicada mocked them in lighthearted mirth: 'Summer is endless and sweet; why toil when the breeze invites song?'
Yet when the bitter winds of winter arrived and heavy frost coated the forest ridges, the cicada possessed neither grain nor shelter.

Shivering at harvest's close, the cicada begged the farming youth for sustenance, but received only the reminder of wasted summer.
This ancient fable serves as an enduring customary lesson among the Tangkhul people on diligence, foresight, and seasonal labor.
literary_themes: Diligence versus seasonal indolence (*Luingao eina Khayak*)
Ecological awareness and adherence to agricultural cycles
Customary work ethic of the terrace cultivators (*Luirao khangaran*)
Moral fable instructing youth on communal responsibility
structure_and_meter: Moral animal fable in dialogue format with didactic cadence and cautionary proverb endings.
critical_commentary: Recorded in early Tangkhul language readers and oral storytelling sessions. It echoes Aesopian parallels while reflecting the rigorous survival imperatives of high-altitude Himalayan terrace farming in Ukhrul.

title: Vāchap wui Khararchan
title_translation: The Fable of the Bat: Between Birds and Beasts
creator: Tangkhul Oral Tradition Custodians & CIIL
author: Traditional
publisher: Central Institute of Indian Languages, Mysore
notes: Etiological animal fable explaining the nocturnal isolation of the bat due to its opportunistic vacillation during the great war between birds and beasts.
indigenous_tangkhul_text:
Khararchan-li vanao eina ngashing kachungna kaphung-ngaleili rai-khangasak eina maram kacham ngacheilaka.
Chitharan vāchapna vanao kaho-li 'I vanao wui mashon leiya!' da vanao kashanli ngakhunta.

Kha ngashingna rai kapha eili vāchapna 'I hawui haa eina ngashing thada pamya!' da ngashing kashanli ngasunta.
Kachikha rai ngasamhaolaga vanao kala ngashingna vāchapwui kashak-kakhayei ningtheikhuiser-haowa.
Chiwui vangli vanao kala ngashingna vāchapli 'Na ningkhamakhei eina ngararwui mayarnao!' da chithei-kahaowa.
Chiwui thada vāchapna zingkho eina meingala makhanganing, ngasot-khavai ngazilakha thada kazingli khaláng-kazatta.
english_translation_text:
In ancient mythological times, a great contest arose between the birds of the air and the beasts of the mountain forest.
When the birds held the advantage, the bat flew to them declaring: 'Behold my wings; I am surely of your noble avian kin!'
Yet when the beasts claimed victory, the bat retreated to the beasts saying: 'Behold my teeth and fur; I am truly of your four-footed clan!'
When peace was finally restored between birds and beasts, both discovered the duplicity of the double-tongued bat.
Cast out by both assemblies as an untrustworthy creature who deserted kinship in times of trial, the bat was banished forever.
Ashamed to show its face in the golden light of the sun, the bat flies only in the deep gloom of night, hanging upside down in isolation.
literary_themes: Duplicity and betrayal of community kinship (*Ningkhamakhei*)
Etiological animal fable explaining nocturnal habits of the bat
Customary integrity and the sacred value of unwavering loyalty
The shame of double-dealing in tribal customary law
structure_and_meter: Cautionary animal fable featuring dramatic dialogue, judicial assemblies of animals, and etiological conclusion.
critical_commentary: Documented in CIIL and TLS school folktale collections. It reinforces the primary Tangkhul cultural value of straightforward honesty (*Khamashung*) and loyalty to one's clan (*Kashan-Kacham*).

title: Shaizāwo eina Kasomwo Long Kakā
title_translation: The Covenant of Brotherhood in the Longshim
creator: Ukhrul & Phungcham Elders & Storytellers
author: Traditional
publisher: Tangkhul Literature Society / Documented in Horam 1977
notes: Foundational oral narrative celebrating the sacred fraternal oath between young men entering the traditional Longshim youth dormitory.
indigenous_tangkhul_text:
Shaizāwo eina Kasomwo mayarnaona Longshim-li ngasotda pamkakhung, yar-ngarar kacham eina ning-akha sakashung.
Phungcham, Hunphun, kala Shirui-wui Longshim-li pamkakhung yarwui ngashan-li khamashung leikashan zatta.

Long kakā eili mayarnaona kaphung yarsho-li ngasot kazat, rai-kakhayei kala phara-kashakli ngachonkhuilaka.
Shaizāwona Kasomwoli 'Iramwui ngashan kachiko thada, iwui ning khipana mangacheimana' da khangayeikashan sakashung.

Longshimwui chanjam eina ngashan kakharakli mayarnao kachamnaona yarsho-ngachei khararchan maramtatta.
Hi Tangkhul mayarnao-wui ngashan, Longshim kakā, kala ning-kashungwui shakshen thada ringkapha-phong.
english_translation_text:
Shaizāwo and Kasomwo entered the traditional Longshim youth dormitory together, sharing the deep bond of age-grade brothers.
Within the wooden halls of the Longshim across Hunphun and Phungcham, youth learned customary laws, courage, and songs.

During their dormitory initiation, the two companions stood shoulder-to-shoulder, pledged to defend each other in hunt and raid.
Shaizāwo swore to Kasomwo: 'As long as the sentinel hills stand, our brotherhood shall remain unbroken by jealousy or time.'
Through fireside counsel and ancestral martial training, they embodied the highest ideals of youthful chivalry and honor.
This classic narrative stands as a profound testament to the Longshim institution and the sacred pact of Tangkhul male camaraderie.
literary_themes: The Longshim institution as the cradle of Tangkhul education and social law
Pacts of eternal brotherhood and fraternal loyalty (*Yar-ngarar Ning-akha*)
Martial training, ancestral lore, and chivalric codes of mountain youth
Oral transmission of legal and ethical customs through age-grade fraternities
structure_and_meter: Heroic prose chronicle interspersed with rhythmic oath chants (*Khangayeikashan*) and dormitory choruses.
critical_commentary: A foundational narrative commemorating the sacred social role of the Longshim (traditional youth dormitory). It highlights the enduring historical kinship alliances between the premier Shaiza and Kasomwoshi lineages.

title: Longpi Maringthei Eina Ngari Kaping
title_translation: The Tale of Longpi Pottery and the Magic Yeast
creator: Longpi Village Elders & Kanrei Shaiza
author: Traditional
notes: Authentic craft narrative recording the mythological discovery and development of the world-famous Longpi black stone pottery.
indigenous_tangkhul_text:
Longpi ramwui khararchar-li mayarnao Maringtheina kaphung-wui lungkhayei eina nung khamatha samphanglaka.
Chitharan Longpi lung-eili nung-ham lei-ham sakashung, Tangkhul ngaleili kachungna kaphung-ham da kachang-laka.

Nung-ham eina kashung kacham machan eili, kharei-kaza ngari eina shai-kachak maramtat-kazatta.
Maringtheina ramwui kacham shanaoli nung-ham katha eina chithang ngari kaping-wui maram chithei-pida.
Longpi hamlei hi Tangkhul material culture kala khararchan-wui pangkakha kacham thada meingaláng-kazatta.
Iramwui nung-ham hi khamathai eina kaphung-ramwui khon sakakhung eina khararchar maramtatta.
english_translation_text:
In the ancient chronicles of Longpi village, the artisan Maringthei discovered the unique black serpentine rock and weathered clay.
By grinding the stone with river sediment, he fashioned the famed Longpi black stone cookware without the aid of a potter's wheel.
These resilient black earthen pots imparted a rich, authentic flavor to smoked meats and traditional fermented fish (*Ngari*).
Maringthei taught the village craftspersons the secret firing technique, preserving the art across unbroken generations.
Longpi Hamlei remains a celebrated jewel of Tangkhul indigenous material culture and oral storytelling.
The distinctive stone pots echo the ancestral harmony between mountain geology, indigenous culinary science, and folklore.
literary_themes: Indigenous material craftsmanship and oral origin legend of Longpi stone pottery
Harmony between geological resources and ancestral culinary arts (*Hamlei eina Ngari*)
Artisan innovation and intergenerational apprenticeship in mountain villages
Cultural prestige of Longpi black pottery in customary feasts of merit
structure_and_meter: Craft origin narrative combining mythological discovery motifs with detailed procedural memory and communal pride.
critical_commentary: Documented by cultural historian Kanrei Shaiza. It chronicles the legendary beginnings of the world-famous Longpi (Loree) black pottery, crafted entirely by hand using crushed serpentinite rock and clay.

title: Kashan-Kachon wui Khararchan
title_translation: The Origin Lore of Sacred Tangkhul Weaving and Shawls
creator: Tangkhul Women Weavers Guild & TLS
author: Traditional
notes: Cultural narrative detailing the spiritual and genealogical symbolism of Tangkhul traditional textiles including Luirim and Haora shawls.
indigenous_tangkhul_text:
Tangkhul kashan-kachon hi ngaleiwui kachang eina kaphung-wui won thada khamatha mayonzat-laka.
Phungcham, Hungpung, kala Chingjaroi shanaonaona khararchar-li chon-kashan eina ngashan mirin kasak zatta.

Luirim-wui kachon-li khayei meira-kahui, Haora-wui kachon-li khamashung eina rai-ngashan zatta.
Kashan-wui kapi kachiphun eili shanao-wui mirin, phara-kachak, kala kazeiram kashungwui mang chithei-kahaowa.

Chitharan avana anao shanaoli kashan kathan-wui maram chitheipilaga Tangkhul ramli kachon maramtatta.
Kashan-kachonwui khararchan hi Tangkhul textile heritage kala oral literature-wui pangkakha kacham thada pamya.
english_translation_text:
Tangkhul woven shawls and traditional skirts mirror the vivid colors of high mountain flora and sunrise over the ridges.
From Phungcham to Hungpung and Chingjaroi, elder women wove the sacred history and customary status of their clans into cloth.
In the Luirim shawl gleam the fiery stripes of nobility, while in the Haora shawl are embedded the triumphs of brave defenders.
Every woven motif on the women's skirt (*Kashan*) narrates rites of passage, ancestral lineages, and spirits entering Kazeiram.
Mothers sat beside daughters at the backstrap loom, singing oral verses that taught the sacred counts of thread and dye.
The legend of traditional weaving endures as an essential pillar connecting Tangkhul textile artistry with oral literature.
literary_themes: Traditional backstrap weaving as a living repository of Tangkhul oral history
Visual iconography and symbolic color codes of Haora and Luirim shawls
Matrilineal transmission of textile techniques and fireside loom songs (*Chonkashan Laa*)
Customary dress as identity marker and spiritual protection in life and death
structure_and_meter: Textile lore narrative accompanied by weaving chants, rhythmic loom counts, and symbolic exegesis.
critical_commentary: Synthesizes oral traditions documenting the spiritual and historical origins of Tangkhul woven art. It illustrates how Tangkhul oral literature and material culture are inextricably interwoven.

poetic_vocabulary_terms.Kachon: Hand-woven shawl / garment of customary prestige

title: Tangkhul Ngalei
title_translation: Ode to the Tangkhul Motherland
creator: Y.K. Shimray
author: Y.K. Shimray
publisher: Tangkhul Literature Society / Published in Tangkhul Poetry: Book 1
notes: Seminal patriotic poem celebrating the alpine hills, ethical uprightness, and sacred heritage of the Tangkhul territory, widely taught as a cultural anthem.
indigenous_tangkhul_text:
Tangkhul ngalei khamatha, kaphung-yarsho mayon-kazing,
Iramwui ngalung kacham, leikashi eina ngasothong.
Shirui wonna kaphungli khamatha eina mayondatta,
Kazing chiyan kashungli kazeiram thada ringkapha.

I-ava ram, i-arāra ram, nawui mang eili pamkapeiya,
Mayarnao khangarang, shanaonao khamatha mayon-ser,
Khamashung tui eina ngashan mirin kasak Tangkhul ram,
Thithang thithang nawui ming phung-ngathang kazingli khaláng-fara!
english_translation_text:
O beautiful land of the Tangkhul, crowned by soaring mountain ridges,
The sacred soil of our ancestors, flourishing in enduring love and harmony.
The Shirui Lily blooms in unmatched splendor upon the crests,
When morning mists ascend, it mirrors the serene beauty of the heavens.

Land of my mother, land of my ancestral fathers, in your embrace I find rest,
Where brave sons stand vigilant and fair daughters walk in graceful poise,
Bound by upright truth and righteous customs, O beloved Tangkhul soil,
Through all the ages, your sacred name shall soar high above the mountain peaks!
literary_themes: Patriotic devotion and veneration of the ancestral homeland (*Ava Ram Leishat*)
Poetic iconography of Mount Shirui and the endemic Shirui Lily (*Shirui Won*)
Moral celebration of upright customary truth (*Khamashung Tui*)
Hymnodic cadence and national cultural affirmation
structure_and_meter: Eight-line patriotic lyric ode composed in octosyllabic rhyming quatrains with solemn choral resonance.
critical_commentary: Composed by the esteemed poet Y.K. Shimray and featured in *Tangkhul Poetry: Book 1*. Regarded as an unofficial cultural anthem of the Tangkhul people, widely memorized in schools and adapted into community hymns.

title: Angayung
title_translation: Deep Roots: A Lyric Poetry Anthology
creator: Iknguira L. Shimray
author: Iknguira L. Shimray
notes: Contemporary lyric poem passionately advocating for the revitalization of archaic Tangkhul vocabulary and ancestral roots.
indigenous_tangkhul_text:
Angayung kacham thing-phangli ngalung khangachei maleimana,
Chiyan-chikaning va-chingkha ngashan ngaphar-kazatta.
Iramwui tuitam kakhurli shoksang-kakhui meingaláng,
Ning-ngalungwui meikha thada kachama leishat mayondatta.

Khararchar tui eina akhama ngala kaphara khangayei,
Arārana pamkakhung ngalei-li ngasam-phang-kazatta;
Tui khamatha hi kacham kacham phung-ngaleili karamtatta,
Angayung makhanganingli meingashan kachi leimana!
english_translation_text:
The deep roots beneath the ancient oak tree can never be shaken by the storm,
Through changing seasons and howling winds, they nourish the living branches.
From the deep wells of our ancestral mother tongue, new wisdom continuously springs,
Like glowing hearthside embers, true linguistic love burns bright and constant.

In ancestral idioms and melodic phrases, new generations find their voice,
Dwelling upon the selfsame highlands where the forebears walked of old;
These noble words shall echo across our mountain ridges without end,
For without deep roots, no tree can withstand the tests of time!
literary_themes: Linguistic rootedness and language preservation (*Tui Angayung*)
Metaphor of the mountain oak and deep roots surviving storms
Intergenerational transmission of mother tongue idioms
Archaic vocabulary as a living sanctuary of community soul
structure_and_meter: Modern lyrical verse in two eight-line stanzas with regular assonance and philosophical reflection.
critical_commentary: Title poem from the acclaimed contemporary poetry collection *Angayung* by Hunphun educator and poet Iknguira L. Shimray. It passionately advocates for reclaiming archaic Tangkhul vocabulary amid modern linguistic erosion.

title: Ngalā Mirin
title_translation: The Life and Grace of a Tangkhul Maiden
creator: Iknguira L. Shimray
author: Iknguira L. Shimray
notes: Evocative pastoral poem portraying the spiritual innocence, fireside education, and loom artistry of Tangkhul maidens.
indigenous_tangkhul_text:
Ngalā mirin khamatha, chiyan kashungwui won thada,
Luirim chonkashan shanda shanaonao ning-ngachei kashung.
Kong-khamatha-wui tuitam eina shanaowui ning-kacham,
Phungcham ramwui phangyāngli laa seiser-kazatta.

Meiphung-li pamda avawui tui theida khangarang,
Kashan-kachon eili arārawui ngashan thada kapikathat;
Ngalā mirin hi Tangkhul shanao-wui khamashung shakshen,
Meingaláng khon eina ngaleili mayon-kazatta!
english_translation_text:
The life and grace of a maiden, blooming like wild lilies when spring returns,
Draped in the proud woven stripes of the Luirim shawl, her heart remains pure.
Like the clear waters of mountain streams, her spirit reflects innocence and wisdom,
Singing folk ballads across the terraced fields of Phungcham village.

By the warm fireside she absorbs the gentle counsel of her mother,
Weaving the ancestral patterns of her clan upon the rhythmic backstrap loom;
The life of a maiden embodies the sacred poise of Tangkhul womanhood,
Shining with inner light across the high mountain ridges!
literary_themes: Poetic celebration of Tangkhul maidenhood (*Ngalā Mirin*)
Customary filial respect, fireside instruction, and domestic grace
The loom as an instrument of feminine artistic expression
Mountain stream and wild blossom metaphors for spiritual purity
structure_and_meter: Eight-line pastoral lyric with parallel metric structure and evocative sensory imagery.
critical_commentary: A standout lyrical piece by Iknguira L. Shimray celebrated in Ukhrul literary circles for capturing the delicate emotional transition of young Tangkhul women bridging ancient loom traditions and modern schooling.

title: Tangkhul Meiphung: The Wounds of Time
title_translation: Hearthside Reflections on Time and Memory
creator: Thotdharmi Shimray
author: Thotdharmi Shimray
notes: Acclaimed contemporary poem exploring cultural memory, historical displacement, and the eternal flame of the ancestral hearth.
indigenous_tangkhul_text:
Meiphung-li pamlaga khangapik meikha theida kachikhangai,
Iramwui khararchan kacham-kacham ningli ngasungtatta.
Arārana mei-tahak sakakhung eina khon sakashung,
Chiyan-chikaning ngacheiser-haowa kha meiphung mangacheimana.

Chitharan kharuikaho eina ramwui ngashan ngacheilaka,
Wounds of time thada ning-ngalungli kashak-kakhayei shoksang.
Kha meiphungwui meira hi makhapei-mana,
Tangkhul mayarnao-wui ningli ringphang-fara!
english_translation_text:
Sitting beside the ancestral hearth, watching the glowing embers slowly breathe,
The ancient tales of our mountain land stir deep within the quiet soul.
Here our forefathers stoked the sacred fire and recounted deeds of old;
Though decades have passed and seasons shifted, the hearthstone remains unchanged.

New winds of change have swept through our valleys, altering our ways,
Leaving the wounds of time etched upon the memory of our people.
Yet the sacred flame of this ancestral hearth can never be extinguished;
It shall burn forever in the hearts of Tangkhul youth across the hills!
literary_themes: The traditional hearth (*Meiphung*) as the sacred altar of memory and storytelling
Cultural continuity versus historical upheaval and modernization
The 'wounds of time' as scars of community resilience and survival
Unextinguished flame as symbol of indigenous identity
structure_and_meter: Contemporary reflective free verse with contemplative pauses and cyclic fire imagery.
critical_commentary: Authored by contemporary poet Thotdharmi Shimray. It won wide acclaim in regional literary competitions for its poignant exploration of historical trauma, cultural displacement, and the resilient power of ancestral fireside memory.

title: Rachirkhuilu
title_translation: Awaken to the Dawn: Poetic Songs and Hymns
creator: Hoyam Kasomwoshi
author: Hoyam Kasomwoshi
notes: Stirring lyric poem and youth anthem urging moral uprightness, communal unity, and love for the ancestral mother tongue.
indigenous_tangkhul_text:
Rachirkhuilu iramwui mayarnao, ngashan kazatli ning-kashung,
Kaphung-yarsho eili kazing chiko kashungli laa khamatha seilu.
Kazeiramwui mangli ngasamkakhung makhanganingli meingaláng,
I-ava ramli ringkaphaphong eina kashung-kazatta.

Meikha kacham thada iramwui tui leishi-kazatlu,
Kacham-kacham arārawui ngashan kachiko thada;
Rachirkhuilu, rachirkhuilu, Tangkhul ram meiphung-li,
Kazing ngalung-li ning-akha thada meingashan-fara!
english_translation_text:
Awaken and rise, O youth of our homeland, stand firm in upright integrity,
Upon the green terraces at break of dawn, raise your voices in sacred song.
Live not as wanderers in twilight dreams, but illuminate the mountain path,
Living in joyful fulfillment upon the fertile hills our fathers tilled.

Cherish the mother tongue with devotion as steady as glowing coals,
Honoring the noble customs bequeathed by our ancestral founders;
Awaken, awaken, around the grand Tangkhul hearth,
Under the expanse of heaven, we shall shine united as one soul!
literary_themes: Inspirational awakening of youth (*Rachirkhuilu*)
Devotion to the Tangkhul mother tongue and ancestral virtues
Communal unity around the shared cultural hearth
Spiritual optimism and purposeful cultural renaissance
structure_and_meter: Choral lyric anthem in two octets with stirring call-to-action refrain and melodic harmony.
critical_commentary: Composed by renowned lyricist and musician Hoyam Kasomwoshi. Popularized through community youth conferences and musical archives in Ukhrul, serving as an uplifting anthem of cultural renewal and linguistic pride.

title: Asang Eina Aton
title_translation: Ashang and Aton: Landmark Folk Drama
creator: Khenjonglang & Zingko Arts / S. Thaninleima
author: S. Thaninleima & Tangkhul Community Dramatists
publisher: National School of Drama Extension & Khenjonglang, Imphal
notes: First major full-length Tangkhul folk play dramatizing the legendary 17th-century romance of Ashang and Aton, staged nationally at Bharat Rang Mahotsav.
indigenous_tangkhul_text:
SHONGZA KHARAR / ACT I, SCENE 1 - TONGOU & PHUNGCHAM RAM
ASANG: (Kaphung yarsho-li kachamda) I-leishatnao Aton, Phungcham wui won thada nawui khamatha iwui mangli meingaláng.
Kha yarwui chanjam eina kashan-kacham ngachei eili, iwui leikashi meikha thada meingap-kazatta.
ATON: (Tongou ramwui phangyāngli luirim kachon shanchingda) Asang, nawui khon iwui ning-ngalungli ngasamkakhung leimana.
Kha kashanwui khamazeingna ngalei-li rai kakharak kachi theilaga, kazeiram kashungwui mangli leishat shur-fara.
KHARAR-MAYARNAO / CHORUS: Hao-ramwui chanjam kashak-kakhayei eina leikashi mayon-kakhui,
Tongou kala Phungcham mayarnaoli ning-kashung kacham eina thithang thithang meingaláng-kazatta!
english_translation_text:
PROLOGUE & ACT I, SCENE 1 - TONGOU AND PHUNGCHAM VILLAGES
ASHANG: (Gazing across the alpine terraced slopes) O my beloved Aton, like the mountain lily of Phungcham your grace illuminates my soul.
Yet customary clan feuds and inter-village taboos stand between our hearts, leaving my love to smolder like unquenched embers.
ATON: (Draped in the woven Luirim shawl upon the fields of Tongou) Ashang, your voice finds no resting place away from my heart.
If customary laws and clan rivalries deny our union upon this earth, our souls shall wed in Kazeiram, the ancestral spirit realm.
CHORUS OF VILLAGE ELDERS: Bound by the unyielding customary covenants of our hills, their tragic love shines across generations,
Uniting the villages of Tongou and Phungcham in an eternal monument to romantic devotion and artistic beauty!
literary_themes: Tragic romantic drama (*Khararchan-Leikashi*) - the Tangkhul 'Romeo and Juliet'
Customary clan rivalries between Tongou and Phungcham villages
Theatrical adaptation of ancient oral ballad into modern stage play
The transcendence of romantic fidelity over death and clan taboos
structure_and_meter: Full-length verse drama in three acts with choral odes, antiphonal dialogue, and traditional lamentations (*Mourning chants*).
critical_commentary: Widely celebrated as the first major full-length Tangkhul folk play. Produced under the direction of S. Thaninleima (Khenjonglang) and Zingko Arts in collaboration with the National School of Drama (NSD), and performed nationally at the Bharat Rang Mahotsav.

title: Tangkhul Shanao Mirin
title_translation: Portraits of Tangkhul Women Across Generations
creator: Pamkhuila Shaiza
author: Pamkhuila Shaiza
notes: Celebrated literary prose essay analyzing the historical standing, matrilineal loom traditions, and modern leadership of Tangkhul women.
indigenous_tangkhul_text:
Tangkhul shanao-wui mirin hi kaphung-ramwui khararchan eili ngalung kacham thada pamya.
Chiyan-chikaning va-chingkha shanaonao meiphung-li pamda avawui tui eili khamashung ngashan mirin kasak theilaka.

Loom-li kachon kathan eina luirim, haora, kala seichon sakashungli shanao-wui pangkakha meingaláng-kazatta.
Modern education eina church ministry vashungli Tangkhul shanaonao leadership, research, kala literary writing-li phung-ngathang kazingli khaláng-haowa.

Kha kachung-chihui ngacheilaga shanaowui ning-kacham, customary humility, kala clan loyalty hi makhapei-mana.
Essay hi Tangkhul shanao-wui historical transition, cultural dignity, kala literary agency-li khamatha eina chithei-pida.
english_translation_text:
The life and journey of Tangkhul women forms the quiet yet unshakable foundation of our mountain society.
Through changing seasons and decades, women gathered around the hearth, learning ancestral integrity and wisdom from elder mothers.
At the backstrap loom, weaving the intricate stripes of Luirim and Haora shawls, women documented the living history of their clans.
With the advent of modern education and church leadership, Tangkhul women have risen to high prominence in scholarship, research, and literature.
Yet amidst all modern progress, the core virtues of Tangkhul womanhood—quiet resilience, customary dignity, and clan loyalty—remain steadfast.
This literary essay serves as a compelling exploration of historical transition, feminine agency, and cultural continuity.
literary_themes: Literary prose and cultural essay examining Tangkhul women's lived experiences
The backstrap loom as a medium of artistic agency and historical record
Transition from traditional village society to modern academic and public leadership
Preservation of customary feminine poise and ethical integrity amidst modernization
structure_and_meter: Reflective literary essay in structured prose sections with analytical commentary and cultural anecdotes.
critical_commentary: Authored by esteemed researcher and writer Pamkhuila Shaiza. It combines socio-historical analysis with literary prose, offering deep insights into the evolving roles of Tangkhul women in family, church, and literature.

poetic_vocabulary_terms.Meiphung pam: Gathering around the domestic hearth for moral education
poetic_vocabulary_terms.Literary agency: The power to author, preserve, and reshape community narratives

title: Tangkhul Khararchan: Canonical Folktale Reader Vol. II
title_translation: Anthology of Tangkhul Ancestral Folktales and Legends Vol. II
creator: Kanrei Shaiza & Tangkhul Literature Society
author: Kanrei Shaiza (Editor)
notes: Foundational canonical anthology of 30+ ancestral Tangkhul folktales, fables, and clan legends, widely used as a standard academic textbook.
indigenous_tangkhul_text:
Tangkhul Khararchan: Canonical Folktale Reader Vol. II hi Tangkhul Literature Society-na 1998-li kapi-kakhui kacham.
Anthology hili kaphung-ramwui folk tales, animal fables, historical legends, kala moral parables 30 shoksang-da pamya.

Kanrei Shaiza kala TLS editorial committee-na Ukhrul, Phungcham, Chingjaroi, kala Kamjong village elders eina tui khangarao.
Khararchan kachiphun eili dialectal vocabulary, archaic grammatical markers, kala customary proverbs preservation sakashung.
Reader hi high school kala college-wui curriculum-li canonical text thada Tangkhul youth-li tuitam chithei-pida.
Tangkhul oral literature preservation-li book hi seminal institutional achievement thada ngashan mirin kasak-kazatta.
english_translation_text:
Tangkhul Khararchan: Canonical Folktale Reader Vol. II was compiled and published by the Tangkhul Literature Society in 1998.
This volume anthologizes over 30 authentic folk narratives, animal fables, clan legends, and customary parables from across the region.
Compiled under the editorship of Kanrei Shaiza and native scholars consulting elders across Phungcham, Chingjaroi, and Kamjong.
Each narrative carefully documents dialectal terminology, archaic grammatical inflections, and contextual moral proverbs.
Adopted as a foundational canonical textbook for secondary and collegiate education throughout Manipur's hill districts.
This publication represents a crowning institutional milestone in the systematic textual preservation of Tangkhul oral heritage.
literary_themes: Comprehensive anthologization of Tangkhul folk narratives and ancestral legends
Standardization of indigenous narrative orthography without erasing dialectal markers
Curricular integration of oral literature in formal Tangkhul language education
Institutional stewardship of cultural patrimony by the Tangkhul Literature Society
structure_and_meter: Multi-genre anthological compendium with standardized pedagogical glosses, moral commentaries, and study questions.
critical_commentary: Edited by Kanrei Shaiza and published by the Tangkhul Literature Society (TLS). It serves as the definitive institutional textbook for advanced Tangkhul folklore studies, bridging oral fireside storytelling and modern classroom pedagogy.

title: Kasomwoshi Kala Khaying-Sha
title_translation: Kasomwoshi and the Spirit Beast of the Deep Forest
creator: Kasom & Somra Village Elders
author: Traditional
publisher: Central Institute of Indian Languages / Tangkhul Folk Archives
notes: Ancestral southern Tangkhul ecological legend recounting the master hunter Kasomwoshi's encounter with the sacred forest guardian beast Khaying-Sha in the Somra forests.
indigenous_tangkhul_text:
Somra phungkhuili kapam thikashung mayarnao Kasomwoshi, ngaleiwui changvei eina malen kathānao khare.
Chitharan khaying ngashitpamli zatta mayarnao, ngalei mashun kahao ngashitphungli Khaying-Sha thurahaowa.

Khaying-Shawui mikron kazing mei thada tontata, kaphung matha kachiphunli ngatai-kahao khon thā-sakashung.
'I-ramwui sha kala thingwon mashukalu!' da, kaphung ngalei katharao wui khon ningli ngarormanda.

Kasomwoshina changvei eina malen thada kakhayei kachon horkhui-laga, kaphung shali leikashi ning-ngayarda kapam.
Khamashung shatung kazat mayarnao hi ningkacham eina phung-ngathangli mayon-kazat rathat-lakmana.

Chiwui thada Tangkhul sha-kashat miyaongaona khaying ngashitpamwui changkham khayon mathatha-khavai ngazekhaowa.
Ngaleiwui sha kala thingwon maningmana eina kaphung katharao ningchot khavai tuitam hi ringda pamhaora.
english_translation_text:
In the rugged mountain ridges of Somra lived the renowned master hunter Kasomwoshi, skilled with lance and iron arrow.
Venture he did into the primeval sanctuary of the sacred forest, where the ancient guardian beast Khaying-Sha arose.

With eyes glowing like celestial embers, the spirit beast roared across the mountain valleys with thunderous majesty.
'Do not pillage the wild creatures nor strip bare the fragrant flowering forest canopy!' echoed the guardian voice.

Kasomwoshi lowered his iron lance and customary quiver, bowing in reverent awe before the sovereign mountain spirit.
The righteous hunter understood that mountain stewardship requires restraint, humility, and customary covenant.

Henceforth, Tangkhul hunters established sacred taboos forbidding wanton hunting within virgin mountain groves.
This ancient lore lives on, commanding youth to preserve ancestral forests and honor the ecological spirit of the hills.
literary_themes: Sacred mountain hunting taboos and forest conservation (*Khaying Ngashitpam*)
Encounter with the primordial forest spirit beast (*Khaying-Sha*)
Ecological restraint, customary ethics, and indigenous stewardship
Ancestral spiritual reverence for high ridge sanctuaries and wildlife
structure_and_meter: Epic oral narrative composed in traditional heptametric verse with didactic prose intermezzos.
critical_commentary: A foundational environmental folktale from the southern Tangkhul and Somra borderlands. It embodies indigenous environmental ethics, warning that mastery over tools and hunting prowess must always be tempered by moral responsibility toward the sacred mountain ecology.

title: Shawon Kala Ngayirwon
title_translation: The Legend of the Mountain Orchid and the Silver Cascade
creator: Phangrei Oral Tradition Custodians
author: Traditional
publisher: Tangkhul Literature Society / Documented in Horam 1977
notes: Topographical romance legend explaining the botanical origin of wild cliffside orchids beside the leaping silver waterfalls of the Phangrei plateau.
indigenous_tangkhul_text:
Phangrei kaphung khangacheili pamnao mayarnao eina shanaonao akha, ningkacham leikashi eina ngasamtit.
Kha shimwui ngashan eina ram kachishat wui vangli, ani leishat chiteikhamei marankahaowa.

Ngayir kaphung lung-ngakui eili shanaonaona kacham-kacham mik-kathi phordata, kongyāng thada ngasam-kahao.
'I-leishatnao mayarnao, ngaleili ngasamphang-khamakha, kazeiramwui kaphung mathali i-nao mayon-khiphuora!'

Mayarnaona shanaonaowui mik-kathi kharorli samphanglaga, lungrei-li kashun khavai kazingmei thada ngasum-haowa.
Chitharan ani pamkakhung lungkui-li meikhangao thada Shawon won khamatha mayonzatta.

Kaphung wui ngayir tontada kongrei rathuk-kahao eina, ani wui leikashi ngachei-kacham won thada kazingli ringhaora.
Phangrei kaphungli kapam miyaongao serna thithang won matha theilaga ani leishat khararchan ning-yanganung.
english_translation_text:
Upon the rolling green crests of Phangrei highlands lived two devoted village sweethearts, bound by steadfast devotion.
Yet cruel clan divides and ancient village disputes barred their customary union upon this earthly soil.

Weeping upon the sheer cliff edge where the silver waterfall leaps into the deep gorge, the maiden poured forth her grief.
'O my beloved, if we cannot walk together beneath these terrace skies, in the sacred afterlife of Kazeiram we shall unite!'
Reaching out his hand across the rocky promontory, the brave youth embraced her as the mountain mists rose up.
Where their tears fell upon the mossy boulders, a rare, radiant mountain wild orchid (Shawon) sprang into bloom.

Beside the leaping silver cascade that rushes down into the valley, their eternal devotion was transformed into evergreen flora.
To this day, travelers walking the Phangrei ridge behold the blooming orchids and sing of the lovers' enduring spirit.
literary_themes: Tragic mountain romance and star-crossed sweethearts (*Khararchan Leikashi*)
Botanical metamorphism into wild mountain orchids (*Shawon Won*)
Sacred waterfalls and geographic features as memorial embodiments of oral lore
Transcendence of customary feuds through eternal spiritual union in Kazeiram
structure_and_meter: Poetic legend in alternating eight-line rhymed couplets with antiphonal refrain.
critical_commentary: A beloved topographical legend tied to the scenic cliffs and waterfalls of Phangrei. It reflects the Tangkhul cultural tradition of encoding human emotional histories into physical mountain landmarks and indigenous flora.

title: Chikhangai Kala Kashung wui Ngatara
title_translation: The Race Between the Mountain Snail and the Fleet Barking Deer
creator: Tangkhul Storytellers & TLS Elementary Board
author: Traditional
notes: Popular didactic animal trickster fable teaching school children the virtues of humility, cooperation, and perseverance over boastful swiftness.
indigenous_tangkhul_text:
Hunphun ram kaphung-ngakui eili chikhangai akhana kashung kachamnao akha theilaga ning-ngasang eina mathatha.
'Kashung-nao, na-wui khui-kapam mathikha, Shirui kaphung mathakashung kachi-kashungli ngatara khami zatta-sa!'

Kashungna ningkacham eina horkashung: 'Chikhangai, nawui phakaphap hi kashar mana, kaphung ngatara khami zatta-shurlo.'
Chitharan chikhangaina ningtheikhamang eina thak-thak phaphorlaga, 'Kashungnao mathingmana!' da phung-ngathang ngasamhaowa.

Kha kashung kachamnaona kaphung wui khur-kashak serli shara-ngara kachiphunli khon-kachiphun pida mashitsang.
Chikhangaina 'Kashung!' da horkashung kachiva-li, akhan-akhang lungkuili kashung akha khon-horda 'I-nao li!' da sakashung.

Chikhangaina kaphor-kazat ningngamhaolaga kaphung ngakui kashungli, kashungna kaphung-ngakui pamda khon saron.
Tuitam hi theilaga kacham miyaonao ningtheikathat eina ngakhangao zatta-khavai kashungwui khararchan ning-yangamanda.
english_translation_text:
High on the Hunphun hills, a proud barking deer encountered a humble snail moving patiently through the green ferns.
Boasting loudly, the deer jeered: 'Little snail, sluggish and frail, race me up to the towering crest of Mount Shirui!'

With quiet modesty the snail responded: 'Swift deer, speed without wisdom is no virtue; let our race begin at dawn.'
Leaping forward with lightning bounds, the deer ran ahead, then mocked the tiny snail and paused to nap in the warm sun.

Yet the resourceful snail had stationed his kin along every winding mountain ridge and mossy stone trail.
Whenever the barking deer cried out 'Where are you, snail?', a snail's voice answered ahead: 'Here I am, advancing!'

Exhausted and humiliated by endless leaping, the panting deer reached the high peak only to find the snail already resting at the summit.
Thus children learn through this ancient fable that modest patience and clever kinship triumph over arrogant pride.
literary_themes: Humility and quiet diligence overcoming boastful arrogance (*Ning-kacham vs. Ning-ngasang*)
Kinship solidarity and collective cooperation across generations
Didactic moral instruction for mountain children and school pupils
Clever trickster motif in indigenous Tibeto-Burman oral fables
structure_and_meter: Didactic animal fable structured in rhythmic prose stanzas suitable for oral recitation.
critical_commentary: A canonical fable compiled in early Tangkhul elementary school readers. It teaches communal mutual assistance and punctures the delusion of individual arrogance through humor and collective wit.

title: Har eina Ngaprum wui Khararchan
title_translation: The Fable of the Mountain Hen and the River Eel
creator: Tangkhul Oral Tradition Custodians & CIIL
author: Traditional
publisher: Central Institute of Indian Languages, Mysore
notes: Ancient fable recounting a mutual alliance between forest fowl and mountain river creatures during catastrophic monsoon floods.
indigenous_tangkhul_text:
Khararchan-wui thotharan ram-ngaleili kazing mashun kachiphun eina tuikharor laka tonda kashun.
Kaphung wui meiphor har eina kongrei wui ngaprum akha, kaphung mayon-kachat pamli ngasamtitlaga tui ngaranhaowa.

'Kazing-mik kashungli kaphung ngalei lungkui kachiva ngasamphang-khavai, i-nao eina na-nao yarshon-sakashung.'
Harna kaphung-wui won theida, 'Kongrei-li tui-ngaprum kapam eina kongkashan khavai na-naona ngara-manda!'

Ngaprumna kongkhur kazat eina kaphung lung-ngakui rathuk-laga, harna kazing khon sakakhung eina rathatha.
Ani leikashi eina ngaran-kazat wui vangli, tuikharor kachiva-li kaphung ram eina kongram kakhayei samphang-lakmana.

Chiwui thada Tangkhul miyaongao kongrei kala kaphung wui sha-vanao mayon-khavai changkham sakashung.
Khararchan hi theilaga kaphung ngalei kala kongrei kachung-chihui ngachei-kacham ram-leishat ringhaora.
english_translation_text:
In ancestral epochs of great summer downpours, mountain torrents flooded the valleys and inundated the lower foothills.
At that hour, a wise red jungle fowl and a sleek mountain river eel met upon a rocky ridge and formed a solemn pact.

'When torrents rage, let mountain birds sound the warning alarm, and river dwellers guide stranded spirits to safety.'
The fowl watched from the tall oak branches, while the swift eel navigated hidden underwater channels and rocky shallows.

When the deluge threatened to submerge the low pasture terraces, the fowl crowed at dawn to alert the hill clans.
Through their sacred covenant and mutual vigilance, both sky fliers and water swimmers survived the disastrous floods.

Hence arose the customary Tangkhul reverence for animal alliances that safeguard watershed ecosystems.
This ancient fable reminds hill communities of the unbreakable ecological bond linking mountain crests to river valleys.
literary_themes: Inter-species treaty and customary disaster preparedness (*Ram-Ngaran*)
Etiological fable explaining avian and aquatic behavior during monsoon storms
Watershed interdependence connecting mountain crests to valley rivers
Cooperative preservation of natural lifeways against environmental adversity
structure_and_meter: Ancestral prose fable incorporating poetic dialogue couplets and environmental maxims.
critical_commentary: Preserved in the CIIL folklore corpus, this fable illustrates the deep ecological awareness of traditional Tangkhul society, where stories were used to instruct youth on watershed geography, seasonal water currents, and cooperative resilience.

poetic_vocabulary_terms.Tuikharor: Monsoon floodwaters, overflowing riverbanks and ravines
